chunks.title: Organizations
chunks.text:
What organizations are

Organizations are the ownership umbrella for projects and teams. An organization may represent a humanitarian program, a mapping community, or any OpenStreetMap group. Each project belongs to one organization. Campaigns can group organizations and projects together.

Viewing an organization

The organization page shows name, slug, logo, description, website, type, subscription information where shown, managers, and teams. You can view an organization as a guest — no login is required.

Team visibility is filtered: organization managers see all teams; other viewers see only public teams.

Types

Organizations have a type such as Free, Discounted, or Full Fee that reflects their subscription arrangement.

Creating, updating, and deleting

- **Who can create:** Only administrators can create organizations.
- **Who can update:** Organization managers and administrators can update their organization.
- **Who can delete:** Only administrators can delete, and only when the organization has no projects. If projects exist, deletion is blocked.
- **Name uniqueness:** Organization names must be unique. Attempting to create a duplicate returns a name-exists error.

Managing organization managers

Each organization has at least one manager.

- Administrators and existing organization managers can manage the manager list.
- Removing the last manager is blocked with a message that at least one manager is required.
- A non-manager cannot manage membership.

Organization and campaign membership

Organizations can be linked to campaigns and vice versa. Duplicate assignments are rejected. This grouping helps filter discovery and show related projects.

Troubleshooting

- **OrgHasProjects (delete blocked):** Remove or reassign projects before deleting the organization.
- **MustHaveAdmin:** You cannot remove the final manager.

See also

- [Teams](../../administrator/02-teams.md)
- [System configuration, i18n, and APIs](../../administrator/04-system-configuration.md)
- [Project permissions and teams](../../project-manager/03-permissions-and-teams.md)

Sources

- Organization service and model, organization detail and management views, and LearnOSM administration guide.

chunks.title: Teams
chunks.text:
What teams are

Teams group contributors. An organization can have many teams. Teams are used to restrict or grant access to mapping, validation, or project management, and to organize communication.

Finding and viewing teams

Browse the teams list and filter by organization, manager, or member. Team visibility matters:

- **Public** teams are discoverable in search.
- **Private** teams only appear to members and organization managers.

Even when you can see a team in the list, its membership details may be limited if it is private and you are not a manager.

Creating a team

- **Who can create:** Organization managers, administrators, or anyone the organization reports as permitted to manage it.
- **Who cannot:** Regular mappers who are not organization managers.

Creation requires an existing organization and a unique name within scope.

Joining a team

Teams define how people join:

- **Open (ANY):** You become a member immediately.
- **Requires approval (BY_REQUEST):** Your request is pending until a team manager approves it. Team managers are notified of the request.
- **Invite-only (BY_INVITE):** You cannot request to join; a manager must invite you, and direct join requests are rejected with a message that the team is invite-only.

You cannot request to join a team you already belong to or have already requested. Some deployments also enforce a level requirement for joining; if you do not meet it, joining is rejected.

Managing members

- **Who can manage:** Team managers, organization managers, and administrators.
- **Who cannot:** Regular members cannot manage membership; attempts return permission errors.

Managers can:

- Add a user by username and set their role (Manager or Member).
- Update a member's role.
- Approve or reject pending requests.
- Send invites and handle accept/reject.
- Remove a user from the team, or the user can leave on their own.

Permission errors include `UserNotTeamManager`, `ApproveJoinError`, and `RemoveUserError`.

Team roles and project access

Teams are linked to projects with a specific role:

- **Mapper** — members can map when the project restricts mapping to teams.
- **Validator** — members can validate when validation is team-restricted (a mapper-only team is not sufficient).
- **Project Manager** — members can manage the project.

A team can be linked to the same project with different roles, but cannot be linked twice with the same role.

See [Project permissions and teams](../../project-manager/03-permissions-and-teams.md) for how these links are configured.

Team announcements

Team managers can broadcast announcements to team members. Delivery respects individual announcement notification preferences; members who disabled announcements may not receive them.

chunks.title: User management and administration
chunks.text:
Viewing users

You can list and search for users by username substring, mapper level, or role, and sort by statistics. Public profiles are viewable without login. Detailed profiles show mapper level, earned badges, statistics such as tasks mapped and validated, countries contributed to, and interests or top projects. Statistics may be refreshed from external counting services when a user maps.

- **Who can search:** Anyone can use the public user search for published information. Filtering by manager is restricted to authenticated organizational users.

Listing and filtering

Administrators can view the full user list and may request more fields than anonymous search.

Blocking

An administrator can set a user to read-only. A read-only user cannot map or validate; permission checks return the blocked reason when such a user tries to lock a task.

- **Who can block:** Administrators only.

> **Needs verification — M-03:** Account deletion anonymizes your profile to a placeholder name, clears personal details, and removes many associated records. Some related data such as messages and chat entries is rewritten or removed, and some aggregate history may be retained for project statistics. The exact scope follows the deployed version and is not detailed in product documentation.

Deleting / anonymizing an account

- **Who can delete:** You can delete your own account. Administrators can delete any account.
- **Who cannot:** Non-administrators cannot delete other users.

Deletion anonymizes your profile to a placeholder like `user_{id}`, clears city, country, email, profile picture, gender, and social identifiers, revokes licenses, removes associated messages, and demotes administrative roles. Some history may be retained for project statistics.

Role elevation

User roles affect system permissions:

- Only administrators can assign the Administrator role. Regular managers cannot escalate someone to Administrator.
- Unknown role values are rejected.

Errors include `OnlyAdminAccess`, `NeedAdminRole`, and `UnknownUserRole` when the caller lacks permission or sends an invalid role.

Administrative sections

The system has additional administrative surfaces such as organization delete, team administration, banner configuration, application keys, and license or mapper-level or badge configuration. These are restricted to administrators and return `OnlyAdminAccess` for other users.

See also

- [Roles and permissions — overview](../../general/05-roles-and-permissions-overview.md)
- [Mapper levels and badges](../../general/07-mapper-levels-and-badges.md)
- [Privacy, security, and data governance](../../administrator/05-privacy-and-security.md)

chunks.title: System configuration, i18n, and APIs
chunks.text:
Languages and translations

The Tasking Manager is available in many languages. The frontend loads the available language list from the system, and the editor switches locale for presets and instructions.

- The system tracks supported languages with codes and language names. The default language fallback is English or the project's default locale.
- Projects store per-language information (name, short description, description, instructions, per-task instructions). See [Configuring a project](../../project-manager/02-configuring-a-project.md).

> **Needs verification — M-13:** Available interface languages and translation completeness vary by deployment. Language fallback behavior when a translation is incomplete is not guaranteed.

Project managers select which languages are available for a project; administrators manage translations.

Licenses and mapper levels

- **Licenses:** Data licenses can be created and listed. Projects may require a specific license before a mapper can work on them. Deleting a license that is still used by a project is blocked.

- **Mapper levels:** Levels such as Beginner, Intermediate, and Advanced are configurable by administrators. Thresholds for progression live in system settings and are checked after mapping or validation activity.

Campaigns, countries, and partners

Campaigns group organizations and projects under a shared theme, countries tag project location, and partners highlight collaborating organizations. Each has an administrative surface for creation and management.

Banners and applications

- **Banners** can show informational or warning messages with agree/disagree and privacy policy links. Only administrators can publish banners.
- **Application keys** support legacy integrations. They are managed through the system administration interface.

A REST API is available under `/api/v2/`. Authenticated requests include a `Token` header; read-only access is available for public resources without login, but mutations require authentication. The API supports locale via `Accept-Language`. Interactive documentation is available where the deployment exposes OpenAPI/Swagger.

Pagination and geographic filtering

List endpoints support pagination with `page` and `per_page` (or similar) parameters. Some endpoints support geographic filters such as bounding boxes. Oversized bounding boxes are rejected with a `BBoxTooBig` error, and self-intersecting geometries are rejected as `SelfIntersectingAOI`.

Grid and task geometry tools

Advanced workflows can interact with task geometries:

- **Intersecting tiles** — Provide an area of interest and a grid to find intersecting task tiles, optionally clipping the grid exactly to the area.
- **Task annotations** — Per-task JSON notes that can be added or updated, used by some project types to attach extra information to tasks.

These are advanced endpoints used by organization workflows and project managers.

Image uploads for project or organization imagery allow certain image formats such as PNG, JPEG, WEBP, and GIF. Other formats are rejected. If no image service is configured on the deployment, uploads are not available.

chunks.title: Privacy, security, and data governance
chunks.text:
Visibility in search and on the project page

Project visibility follows the same rules everywhere: search listings, map view, task grid, and downloads all enforce the same check. See [Private projects and access control](../../general/06-private-projects-and-access-control.md) for the full allowed set. Anonymous users never see private or draft projects.

Authentication

The Tasking Manager authenticates you via your OpenStreetMap account using OAuth. You grant limited access in an OSM consent screen before the system receives a session. That session authorizes your editor to save changes to OpenStreetMap under your OSM account.

Roles and team governance

- **Who can elevate roles:** Only administrators can assign the Administrator role to another user (error `NeedAdminRole` if you lack permission, `OnlyAdminAccess` or `UnknownUserRole`/`UnknownAddRole` if the role value is invalid).
- **Who can manage organizations and teams:** See [Organizations](./01-organizations.md) and [Teams](./02-teams.md).
- **Who is blocked:** Users set to read-only by an administrator cannot map or validate. See [User management and administration](./03-user-management.md).

Data retention and account deletion

> **Needs verification — M-03:** Account deletion anonymizes your profile to a placeholder name, clears personal details, and removes many associated records. Some related data such as messages and chat entries is rewritten or removed, and some aggregate history may be retained for project statistics. The exact scope follows the deployed version and is not detailed in product documentation.

Deleting your own account, or an administrator deleting another account, follows a transactional anonymization. Not all historical mapping contributions are removed.

File uploads

Uploads of imagery or organization logos allow only a small set of image types, such as `png`, `jpeg`, `webp`, and `gif`. Requests with other types return `UnsupportedFile`. If the deployment has not configured an image service, the error `UndefinedImageService` is returned. Uploads must include a filename; otherwise `MissingFilename` is returned.

External service CSRF

Integrations that fetch statistics from external services use a CSRF-aware flow that fetches a token, includes `Referer` and `Origin`, and retries once on a 403 where supported. If no CSRF token is offered by the external service, the request proceeds without it.

> **Needs verification — M-05:** Partner organizations and their visibility on the project or campaign pages depend on the deployment. Some partner fields are managed only by administrators.

Notification privacy

Message delivery respects your notification preferences. You can choose to suppress categories such as mentions, team announcements, and validation notices. Suppressed categories are not delivered to your inbox or by email.

What is Tasking Manager?

Tasking Manager is the HOT tool that divides an area of interest into tasks to coordinate collaborative mapping on OpenStreetMap, preventing overlap and tracking quality via validation. The LearnOSM Tasking Manager Mapper Guide and Administrator Guide both open by describing the Tasking Manager as the essential coordinator between OpenStreetMap (the data), the Tasking Manager (the workflow), and an editor such as iD/JOSM/Rapid.

What's the difference between a beginner, intermediate, and advanced project?

Under **Edit project → Metadata/Permissions** an administrator sets the displayed difficulty and who can actually access the project. A **Beginner** project is open to any mapper, including those with fewer than 250 changesets; **Intermediate** and **Advanced** restrict access to mappers who meet a higher mapping level or team membership. Access is enforced via teams and levels.

chunks.title: What the Tasking Manager is and how it fits the OSM ecosystem
chunks.text:
What it does

The Tasking Manager is a coordination tool for mapping in OpenStreetMap. A project manager defines an area of interest that needs mapping, the system divides it into smaller tasks, and teams of mappers and validators work through those tasks. The project page shows which areas still need mapping and which have been reviewed for quality.

It is free and open source software, originally built for the Humanitarian OpenStreetMap Team (HOT) and now used by many communities. Well-known deployments include the HOT Tasking Manager, TeachOSM, OpenStreetMap Indonesia, OpenStreetMap US, and others for OpenHistoricalMap and regional groups.

How it fits the OSM ecosystem

- **OpenStreetMap** is the database of geographic information. Edits you make through the Tasking Manager are saved to OSM.
- **The Tasking Manager** is the coordinator — it tracks who is working on what and the state of each task.
- **Editors** such as iD, JOSM, and Rapid do the actual editing. They are launched from the Tasking Manager with the correct area and changeset comment.

The high-level workflow

1. An administrator creates and publishes a mapping project for an area.
2. A mapper selects a task, locks it, completes the requested features, and marks it as mapped.
3. A validator reviews mapped tasks and marks them as validated or sends them back for more work.
4. Contributors and managers monitor progress on the project's statistics and activity.

See the [Learn section](../../general/01-what-is-tasking-manager.md) in the application for video tutorials and links to LearnOSM guides.

Where to get help

- **Inside the Tasking Manager:** Use the Learn pages, project instructions, and the project's Questions and Comments thread to contact the project manager.
- **Outside:** Refer to LearnOSM coordination guides, OSM Wiki, and HOT working groups. Map features and tagging are explained in the [OSM concepts](./02-osm-concepts-for-tasking-manager-users.md) guide.

See also

- [OSM concepts for Tasking Manager users](./02-osm-concepts-for-tasking-manager-users.md)
- [Finding work: project discovery and filtering](./08-search-and-discovery.md)

Sources

- Official documentation, LearnOSM Tasking Manager overview, OSM Wiki Tasking Manager.

chunks.title: OSM concepts needed to use the Tasking Manager
chunks.text:
The OSM data model in one paragraph

OpenStreetMap represents real-world features as nodes, ways, and relations tagged with key=value pairs. When you map with the Tasking Manager you are adding those tags to the shared OSM database. Your edits become visible to all OSM users and data consumers after you save.

Changesets and the project hashtag

Every save you make in your editor creates a **changeset**. The Tasking Manager configures each project with a **changeset comment** that includes a project hashtag like `#hotosm-project-1234`. Keep that hashtag in your changeset comment — it lets the community find the edits for a project and powers statistics that track contributions.

> **Good practice:** Copy the suggested comment from the project Instructions tab, add a short description of what you did, and include the source you used. Do not remove the hashtag.

Tagging what the project asks for

Projects specify **mapping types** such as roads, buildings, waterways, or land use. Tagging guidance comes from the project's instructions and from the OSM Wiki Map Features. Common expectations:

- **Buildings** are traced as closed polygons and tagged as buildings.
- **Roads** are traced as lines with road classifications appropriate to the local context.
- **Waterways** include rivers and streams, following local imagery and ground knowledge.

If the project highlights private projects or restricted areas, only map what the instructions describe; do not add unrelated features.

Imagery, sources, and attribution

Use the imagery the project suggests when it is available, or a sensible fallback. Record the source as the instructions request. High-resolution imagery makes it easier to identify buildings and roads; if the imagery is cloudy or unusable you can mark the task as having bad imagery rather than guessing.

Quality checks and OSMCha

After mapping, experienced contributors review work. OSMCha is an external tool that lets validators inspect changesets filtered by hashtag or project. Projects may link an OSMCha filter to help quality assurance.

See also

- [Task states and lifecycle](./03-task-states-and-lifecycle.md) — what happens to your task after you mark it mapped.
- [Tagging, presets, and quality assurance](../../validator/03-quality-assurance-and-tagging.md)

Sources

- OSM Wiki Map Features, Changeset, Quality Assurance, HOT, and LearnOSM beginner/remote guides.

chunks.title: Task states, transitions, and history (authoritative)
chunks.text:
Task states, transitions, and history (authoritative)

This is the authoritative reference for task states in the Tasking Manager. Workflow guides link here instead of repeating the table.

The eight task states

| State | What it means for you |
|---|---|
| **Ready** | No one is working on it yet. It can be locked for mapping. |
| **Locked for mapping** | Someone is actively mapping it. No one else can lock it. |
| **Mapped** | A mapper finished and marked it complete. Ready for validation. |
| **Locked for validation** | A validator is reviewing it. |
| **Validated** | A validator confirmed the mapping is satisfactory. |
| **Invalidated** | A validator found issues and sent it back. It can be mapped again. |
| **Bad imagery** | A mapper reported that the imagery prevents mapping (clouds, blur, no coverage). |
| **Split** | The original task was divided into smaller tasks and no longer appears as a single unit. |

How tasks move between states

- **Ready or Invalidated → Locked for mapping** when a mapper locks a task that they are permitted to map and have no other lock.
- **Locked for mapping → Mapped, Bad imagery, or Ready** when the mapper submits after saving to OSM, reports bad imagery, or stops without completing (reverting to the prior state).
- **Mapped, Bad imagery, or Invalidated → Locked for validation** when a validator who is permitted to validate and who did not do the original mapping locks it.
- **Locked for validation → Validated or Invalidated** when the validator finishes review. Invalidated tasks return to the mapping queue.
- **Any locked task → prior state** if the mapper or validator stops without submitting.
- The system can also auto-release a stale lock, returning the task to its prior state. See [Comments, task history, and managing your lock](../../mapper/05-comments-history-and-lock-management.md).

All other transitions are not allowed. The interface only offers the actions that are valid for the current state.

One-lock rule

You can only have **one task locked at a time** in total — mapping and validation share a single lock budget. Holding a mapping lock prevents you from locking another task for mapping *or* for validation until you finish or release the first lock, and vice-versa. The system checks your current locks before granting a new one. If you try to lock a second task you will receive `UserAlreadyHasTaskLocked` (403) and must finish or release the first lock.

chunks.title: Task states, transitions, and history (authoritative)
chunks.text:
Task history

Every lock, state change, comment, extension, and automatic release is recorded in the **task history**, visible on the task. The history uses eight action types (authoritative `TaskAction` enumeration from `backend/models/postgis/task.py`):

| Action | What you see |
|---|---|
| **Locked for mapping** | You (or another mapper) locked the task to start mapping. |
| **Locked for validation** | A validator locked the task to start review. |
| **State change** | The task moved to a new state (for example Ready → Mapped, or Mapped → Validated). |
| **Comment** | Someone left a comment without changing the state; @-mentions may trigger a notification. |
| **Auto-unlocked for mapping** | The system released a stale mapping lock automatically, returning the task to its prior state. |
| **Auto-unlocked for validation** | The system released a stale validation lock automatically, returning the task to its prior state. |
| **Extended for mapping** | The mapper extended the lock duration while still holding it. |
| **Extended for validation** | The validator extended the lock duration while still holding it. |

You can follow a task's history to see who worked on it, what they did, and why it returned to the queue.

Progress

Project-level progress bars and percentages are derived from task counts — mapped plus validated over total tasks minus bad imagery — not from manual edits. They update automatically when tasks change state.

Restrictions and edge cases

- A task that has been split cannot be merged back together; the original task remains in the Split state and the new smaller tasks take its place.
- A task marked Bad imagery is excluded from the percent-mapped denominator until it is reset by a project manager.

See also

- [Mapping a task](../../mapper/03-mapping-a-task.md)
- [Validating tasks](../../validator/01-validation-workflow.md)
- [Error codes and troubleshooting](./13-error-codes-and-troubleshooting.md)

Sources

- Tasking Manager task model, validator and mapping services, and LearnOSM tasking guides.

chunks.title: Project status and lifecycle (authoritative)
chunks.text:
Project status and lifecycle (authoritative)

This is the authoritative reference for project status. Other guides link here.

Project status

| Status | What you see |
|---|---|
| **Draft** | Only the author, organization managers, assigned team managers, and administrators can view it. It does not appear in public search for regular mappers. |
| **Published** | Visible to mappers according to its access rules. This is the normal working state. |
| **Archived** | Kept for history but no longer presented as active work. Tasks remain as they were. |

Publishing requirements

A project cannot be published unless its default language information is fully filled in: name, short description, description, and instructions must be provided, and at least one mapping type and editor must be selected, and it must belong to an organization. If any required field is missing, the publish action fails with a message about the missing information.

Deletion and archiving

- **Archiving** does not delete tasks or history; it simply marks the project as no longer active.
- **Deletion** is only allowed when the project has no completed work — that is, every task is still in the Ready state. If any task has been mapped, validated, or marked as bad imagery, deletion is blocked. Only organization managers and administrators can delete.

Sandbox and database variants

Some projects are marked as **sandbox** for practice; they behave like regular projects but are intended for learning. The underlying database is normally OpenStreetMap; a small number of deployments use a separate database such as OpenHistoricalMap for historical mapping.

See also

- [Creating a new project](../../project-manager/01-creating-a-project.md)
- [Managing a project through its lifecycle](../../project-manager/04-managing-a-project.md)

Sources

- Project model, project administration service, and LearnOSM administration guide.

chunks.title: Roles and permissions — overview and reference (authoritative)
chunks.text:
Roles and permissions — overview and reference (authoritative)

This is the authoritative reference for who can do what. Workflow guides summarize only the permissions relevant to that workflow and link back here for the full tables.

Roles

- **Guest (not logged in)** — Can browse public, published projects and view organization and user profiles. Cannot lock tasks, comment, or edit.
- **Mapper** — Logged-in user who can map when permitted. All authenticated users start as mappers unless otherwise assigned.
- **Validator** — Experienced mapper permitted to review mapped tasks. Validators are mappers with additional validation permission on a project.
- **Project manager** — Member of a project team with manager role for that project, or the project author. Can edit and manage the project.
- **Organization manager** — Manages an organization and can create projects under it.
- **Team manager** — Manages a team and its membership.
- **Administrator** — Can manage organizations, teams, users, licenses, and system configuration. Administrators and project managers bypass some project restrictions.

A single user can hold several of these at once (for example, organization manager and validator).

Who can view a project

- **Public + published** → anyone, including guests.
- **Private + published** → only the project author, users on the allowed list, members of assigned teams, organization managers for that organization, and administrators.
- **Draft** → only the author, organization managers, assigned team managers, and administrators. Regular mappers cannot view drafts at all.

Requests without permission receive a 403 error. See [Private projects and access control](./06-private-projects-and-access-control.md) for the full matrix.

chunks.title: Roles and permissions — overview and reference (authoritative)
chunks.text:
Who can map

A mapper can lock a task for mapping when **all** of these are true:

1. They are not blocked and are logged in.
2. The project is published.
3. They have no other task currently locked (mapping and validation share a single lock budget — see [One-lock rule](./03-task-states-and-lifecycle.md#one-lock-rule)).
4. Any required data license for the project has been accepted.
5. Their mapper level meets the project's minimum mapping level, if one is set.
6. If the project restricts mapping to teams, they belong to a team assigned as Mappers (or Validators or Project Managers) for that project.
7. If the project is private, they are on the allowed list or in an assigned team, or they are an organization manager or administrator.

Who cannot: guests cannot map; blocked users cannot map; users who have not accepted a required license cannot map; users below the required level cannot map; users not in a required team cannot map; users not on the allowed list for a private project cannot map; users who already have a task locked cannot lock another. Each failure returns a distinct error such as `UserNotAllowed`, `ProjectNotPublished`, `UserAlreadyHasTaskLocked`, or `UserNotAcceptedLicense`. If the task is not in a mappable state (for example it is already validated), the error is `InvalidTaskState`.

Who can validate

Validation follows a similar decision but checks validation-specific gates:

1. The mapper is not blocked and is logged in.
2. The project is published.
3. They have no other task locked (mapping and validation share a single lock budget — see [One-lock rule](./03-task-states-and-lifecycle.md#one-lock-rule)).
4. Required license accepted.
5. Their mapper level meets the project's minimum validation level (often Intermediate by default).
6. If validation is restricted to teams, they belong to a team assigned as Validators or Project Managers for that project. A team assigned only as Mappers is not sufficient.
7. Private project allowed-list/team check as above.

Additionally, validators **cannot validate their own mapping** unless they are an administrator — only administrators may validate their own tasks. Project managers, organization managers, and other validators cannot self-validate, even though they can validate tasks mapped by other users. Attempting to self-validate without administrator permission returns `CannotValidateMappedTask`. The distinction is: being able to *validate tasks* on a project (level/team/license) does not grant the ability to validate *your own* task. The task must be in Mapped, Bad imagery, or Invalidated to be locked for validation; otherwise the error is `NotReadyForValidation`.

chunks.title: Roles and permissions — overview and reference (authoritative)
chunks.text:
Teams and levels

- **Team-gated (TEAMS)** means the project manager assigned at least one team to the relevant role. If the project says mapping is team-restricted but no mapper team is assigned, the project cannot be saved.
- **Level-gated** compares your mapper level ordering to the project's required level. Being below the threshold blocks lock with `UserNotCorrectMappingLevel`. Levels are described in [Mapper levels and badges](./07-mapper-levels-and-badges.md).

Organization and project-manager bypass

Project author, organization managers, assigned team managers with the Project Manager role for that project, and administrators are treated as managers for that project and bypass team, level, and private-list checks when viewing or managing the project.

What happens if you try

All permission failures return a JSON error with a stable `SubCode` and a 403 or 409 status. See [Error codes and troubleshooting](./13-error-codes-and-troubleshooting.md) to translate a SubCode into what went wrong and what to do next.

chunks.title: Private projects and access control (authoritative)
chunks.text:
Private projects and access control (authoritative)

This is the authoritative reference for private and draft visibility.

What private means

A project can be marked **private** so that only a defined set of people can see and work on it. Private projects do not appear in public search results or map views for other users, and attempts to open their task grid or download their task data return a 403 error for unauthorized users.

Who can see and work on a private, published project

The allowed set is the union of:

- Users explicitly on the **allowed list** for that project,
- Members of **teams assigned to the project** (any role configured for the project),
- The **project author**,
- **Organization managers** for the project's organization,
- **Administrators**.

Everyone else — including logged-in mappers who are not on the list or in an assigned team — receives a Private Project error and cannot view the project, its tasks, or its downloads. Guests cannot view private projects at all.

Draft projects are unpublished. Only the author, organization managers, assigned team managers, and administrators can view a draft. Regular mappers and guests do not see drafts in search and receive an error if they try to open one.

Practical consequences

- **Search and discovery:** private and draft projects are excluded from public listings.
- **Task grid:** the grid can only be fetched for projects you are permitted to view.
- **Downloads:** task grid and data downloads follow the same visibility rules as the project page.

Restrictions and edge cases

- A project that restricts mapping or validation to teams must have at least one team assigned to the appropriate role; otherwise it cannot be saved.
- Being on the allowed list for a private project does not automatically grant validation permission — the project's level and team rules still apply when you try to lock a task.

See also

- [Roles and permissions — overview](./05-roles-and-permissions-overview.md)
- [Reading the project page and selecting a task](../../mapper/02-project-page-and-task-selection.md)

chunks.title: Mapper levels, badges, and progression (authoritative)
chunks.text:
Mapper levels describe experience. Typical deployments use Beginner, Intermediate, and Advanced. Each level has an ordering — a higher level satisfies any lower-level requirement. Projects may set a minimum mapping level or minimum validation level; you must meet or exceed that level to lock a task for the relevant action.

- **Who can view levels:** Anyone can view level definitions.
- **Who can change levels:** Only administrators can create or edit levels.
- **Who can move between levels:** The system updates levels automatically based on your mapping statistics after you complete tasks. Lower levels cannot self-promote arbitrarily.

Badges are achievements earned by meeting statistical milestones. They are assigned automatically by the system when your statistics satisfy their requirements. You can view badges assigned to you.

> **Needs verification — M-02:** Badge names, icons, and the exact statistics required to earn each badge vary by Tasking Manager deployment. This guide describes how badges work in general; check your profile page or ask an administrator for the catalog used here.

How level progression works

After you finish mapping or validation, the system checks whether new badges have been earned and whether your level threshold is met. If so, your level advances. On some deployments, level changes may involve an approval or voting step.

> **Needs verification — M-04:** Promotion between mapper levels can involve an approval or voting step on some deployments. Who can vote and what quorum is required is configuration-dependent and not documented in the sources used for this guide.

Restrictions

- A project can require Intermediate for validation while allowing Beginner for mapping — the two thresholds are independent.
- Your level is checked each time you try to lock a task; being promoted does not retroactively affect locks you already hold.

See also

- [Roles and permissions — overview](./05-roles-and-permissions-overview.md) — how level gates are evaluated.
- [Validating tasks](../../validator/01-validation-workflow.md)

Sources

- Mapping level and badge models, mapping level and badge services, user service, and profile views.

chunks.title: Finding work: project discovery and filtering
chunks.text:
How do I find a project?

Go to Explore Projects. By default you see published projects you are permitted to view. Draft and private projects you are not permitted to see do not appear.

How do I search?

- **Text search:** Type part of a project name or description, or a project identifier such as `#1234`, and press Enter. Search looks inside project descriptions and matches identifiers.
- **Browse the map:** Switch to the map view to see where projects are located. Clusters show how many projects are in an area — zoom in to see individual projects.

How do I filter projects?

Use the filters above the project list. You can combine filters:

- **Difficulty:** Easy, Moderate, or Challenging — set by the project manager to guide mappers of different experience levels.
- **Status:** Published or Archived.
- **Priority:** Urgent, High, Medium, or Low.
- **Mapping types:** Roads, Buildings, Waterways, Land Use, or Other — what the project asks you to map.
- **Campaign, Organization, Country, Interests:** Groupings chosen by project managers.

Filters respect visibility: a private project may exist but still not appear unless you are on its allowed list or in an assigned team.

How do I sort and export results?

Sort the list by priority, creation date, or last update. You can also download the current result as a data file for analysis outside the Tasking Manager.

Prerequisites and restrictions

- No login is needed to browse public projects.
- Login is needed to see private projects you have access to and to lock tasks.
- You cannot view draft projects unless you are the author, an organization manager, an assigned team manager, or an administrator.

See also

- [What the Tasking Manager is](./01-what-is-tasking-manager.md)
- [Reading the project page and selecting a task](../../mapper/02-project-page-and-task-selection.md)

Sources

- Project search service, home view, project filter components, and LearnOSM discovery guides.

chunks.title: Messages, notifications, and project Q&A
chunks.text:
Inbox and notifications

Your inbox holds messages sent to you by the system and by other contributors. Each message has a subject, body, project and task context where applicable, and a read state. A badge shows how many unread messages you have.

- **Who can read:** Only you can read your inbox. You cannot read another user's inbox.
- **Who can be notified:** The system sends messages such as welcome notes when you join, validation notes when your mapped task is reviewed, mentions when someone tags you, and broadcasts from project managers to all contributors.

> **Needs verification — M-09:** Notifications are available in an inbox. Whether updates are delivered by live push or periodic polling depends on the deployment.

Notification preferences

In your settings you can choose which kinds of notifications you receive — for example mentions, project activity, team broadcasts, task comments, and validation or invalidation of tasks you mapped. Disabling a category suppresses both inbox delivery and email for that category. You can change these at any time.

Email

If you provided an email address, the system can also send email alerts for inbox messages, depending on your preferences and whether your email address is verified. Verification uses a token sent to your email. Well-known templates exist for welcome and validation/invalidation notes.

Project Q&A and @-mentions

- **Project questions and comments:** From a project's detail page, any authenticated user who can view the project can post a question or comment. Project managers can respond there.
- **Task comments and @-mentions:** When working on a task you can leave a comment. If you mention another user with `@username`, that user receives a mention notification, unless they mentioned themselves or they have disabled that category. Guests cannot post comments.

Who can message contributors

Project managers can send a broadcast message to all contributors who have mapped or validated on that project. The message is formatted from Markdown and sent as a background job. Only managers for that project can do this; other mappers cannot broadcast to contributors.

See also

- [Comments, task history, and managing your lock](../../mapper/05-comments-history-and-lock-management.md)
- [Error codes and troubleshooting](./13-error-codes-and-troubleshooting.md)

Sources

- Messaging and notification services, message and notification models, messages and notifications views, comments components, and LearnOSM tasking guides.

chunks.title: Statistics, contributions, and activity
chunks.text:
Project progress

Each project shows totals for how many tasks are mapped, validated, or marked as having bad imagery, alongside the total number of tasks. Percentages are calculated automatically from task states: mapped plus validated over total tasks minus tasks with bad imagery. You do not need to update these numbers yourself.

Contribution timeline

The project's timeline shows per-day activity for mapped, validated, and invalidated tasks, with cumulative totals over time. Managers and mappers can use this to see how the project is advancing.

Leaderboard and activity feed

A leaderboard lists contributors who have mapped or validated on the project, and an activity feed shows recent state changes — excluding plain comments — paginated ten at a time. Comments are available separately on each task.

Task history

Each task has its own history showing locks, state changes, comments, and automatic releases, in order. You can use this to understand who did what and when.

User statistics

Your profile shows how many tasks you have mapped, validated, or had invalidated, which countries you have contributed to, and which recent projects you have worked on. More detailed statistics can incorporate object counts from external statistics services and changeset counts, updated periodically when you map.

Downloading project areas and task grids

For projects you are permitted to view, you can download the project's area of interest and its task grid as GeoJSON files. These downloads follow the same visibility rules as the project page.

See also

- [Task states and lifecycle](./03-task-states-and-lifecycle.md)
- [Comments, task history, and managing your lock](../../mapper/05-comments-history-and-lock-management.md)

Sources

- Statistics and project services, task model, status and timeline components, and user detail views.

chunks.title: Interests, favorites, and recommended projects
chunks.text:
Interests describe topics you care about, such as disaster response or community mapping. You can select interests in your profile, and project managers can assign interests to projects.

- **Who can set your interests:** You can set your own interests when authenticated. Guests cannot save interests.
- **Who can set project interests:** Project managers can assign interests to their projects.

Interests cannot be deleted while they are still assigned to a user or a project.

Favorites

You can mark a project as a favorite to save it to your list. Only authenticated users can favorite; guests cannot. You can list the projects you have favorited from your profile.

Recommended and similar projects

When viewing a project, you may see a list of similar projects. Similarity considers factors such as mapping types, country, categories, difficulty, and language. Only published projects are considered for recommendations. If fewer than two published projects exist, no recommendations are shown.

Similarity is computed from a matrix that is cached for a period of time; recently created projects may not appear immediately.

Restrictions

- Interests that are still in use cannot be removed via the administration interface.
- Recommendations never include private or draft projects you are not permitted to view.

See also

- [Finding work: project discovery and filtering](./08-search-and-discovery.md)
- [Creating an account, logging in, and managing your profile](../../mapper/01-account-and-login.md)

Sources

- Interests and recommendation services, project model, and interests, favorites, and similar-projects components.

chunks.title: Exporting data: HOT Export Tool, Overpass, and downloads
chunks.text:
Downloading project areas and task grids

For any project you are permitted to view, you can download:

- **Area of interest (AOI)** — the overall boundary of the project as GeoJSON.
- **Task grid** — the task polygons as GeoJSON, either as a file or inline preview.

Use the Download buttons on the project page. Private and draft projects require permission, just like viewing the project page itself.

Exporting mapped data

Mapped data can be exported for use outside the Tasking Manager:

- **HOT Export Tool** — Project managers configure which mapping types (roads, buildings, waterways, land use) are expected. Downloads are organized by project and mapping type, with separate files per geometry type (points, lines, polygons) and format (GeoJSON, shapefile, KML), stored under a project-specific path. You may be asked to wait briefly while the export prepares; on failure a message is shown and you can retry.
- **Overpass** — Advanced users can query OpenStreetMap data directly with the Overpass API using a polygon from the project geometry. Note: the shared public Overpass instance can be heavily loaded; keep query volume modest — community guidance treats fewer than 10,000 queries per day as safe — and set a descriptive User-Agent header when querying programmatically.

Downloading task areas for your editor

You can download the geometry of one or more tasks as GPX or OSM XML to side-load into your editor or for offline use. These downloads are available from the task or project context where shown.

Licenses

Some projects require you to accept a data license before you can map. If a license is required and you have not accepted it, mapping is blocked until you accept. This also governs the reuse of exported data from that project.

> **Needs verification — M-08:** The downloadable project list (CSV) includes core project attributes such as identifier, name, status, priority, difficulty, organization, and progress. The exact column set follows the deployed API and may vary slightly.

See also

- [Reading the project page and selecting a task](../../mapper/02-project-page-and-task-selection.md)
- [Editors and imagery](../../mapper/04-editors-imagery-and-gpx.md)
- [OSM concepts for Tasking Manager users](./02-osm-concepts-for-tasking-manager-users.md)

Sources

- Overpass service, project service, license service, download components, LearnOSM administration guide, and OSM Wiki Overpass API.

chunks.title: Error codes and troubleshooting (authoritative error surface)
chunks.text:
Error codes and troubleshooting (authoritative)

This is the authoritative reference for errors. Other guides link to the relevant anchor here instead of repeating the catalog.

How errors are reported

The application returns HTTP status codes with a JSON body containing a stable `SubCode` and a human message. The message text may change, but the SubCode stays the same.

- **400 Bad request** — InvalidData, MustBeFeatureCollection, InvalidMultipolygon, PropertyNotFound, BBoxTooBigError, SelfIntersectingAOI, etc.
- **401 Unauthorized** — InvalidToken, ExpiredToken, BadSignature, UnableToAuth, UserNotTeamManager, LoginToFilterManager.
- **403 Forbidden** — InvalidTaskState, LockBeforeUnlocking, TaskNotOwned, UserAlreadyHasTaskLocked, UserNotAllowed, ProjectNotPublished, PrivateProject, ProjectNotFetched, NotPermittedToCreate, UserPermissionError, OnlyAdminAccess, NeedAdminRole, DeletePermissionError, HasMappedTasks, CannotValidateMappedTask, NotReadyForValidation, NotLockedForValidation, UndoPermissionError, LockToSplit, SmallToSplit, SplitGeoJsonError, SelfIntersectingAOI, etc.
- **404 Not found** — ProjectNotFound, TaskNotFound, TeamNotFound, UserNotFound, and other resource not-found codes.
- **409 Conflict** — UserLicenseError, NameExists.

See `docs/developers/error_code.md` for the full table.

I cannot lock a task for mapping

- **`UserAlreadyHasTaskLocked` (403)** — You already have a task locked elsewhere. Finish or release that lock first. See [Comments, task history, and managing your lock](../../mapper/05-comments-history-and-lock-management.md).
- **`InvalidTaskState` (403)** — The task is not in a mappable state. Only tasks that are Ready or Invalidated can be locked for mapping. See [Task states and lifecycle](./03-task-states-and-lifecycle.md).
- **`ProjectNotPublished` (403)** — The project is still a draft. Only the author, organization managers, or assigned team managers can view drafts.
- **`PrivateProject` (403)** — You do not have permission to view this private project. See [Private projects and access control](./06-private-projects-and-access-control.md).
- **`UserLicenseError` (409)** — You must accept the project's data license first.
- **`UserNotCorrectMappingLevel` / permission errors** — Your mapper level or team membership does not satisfy the project's requirements. See [Roles and permissions — overview](./05-roles-and-permissions-overview.md).

chunks.title: Error codes and troubleshooting (authoritative error surface)
chunks.text:
I cannot lock a task for validation

- **`CannotValidateMappedTask` (403)** — You cannot validate a task you mapped yourself. Only administrators may validate their own tasks — project managers, organization managers, and other validators receive this error when they try. See [Validating tasks](../../validator/01-validation-workflow.md#self-validation-guard).
- **`NotReadyForValidation` (403)** — The task must be Mapped, marked Bad imagery, or Invalidated before it can be locked for validation.
- **`UserAlreadyHasTaskLocked` (403)** — You already hold a lock; release it before validating another task.

I cannot unlock or submit

- **`TaskNotOwned` / `LockBeforeUnlocking` (403)** — You are trying to unlock a task you do not hold, or that is not in the locked state you hold. Only the lock holder can submit.
- **`NotLockedForValidation` (403)** — The task is not locked for validation by you.

I cannot split a task

- **`LockToSplit` (403)** — The task must be locked for mapping by you.
- **`SmallToSplit` (403)** — The task is already too small.
- **`SplitOtherUserTask` (403)** — You are trying to split a task held by someone else.
- **`SplitGeoJsonError` (403)** — The generated split geometry is invalid.

Imagery issues

If imagery fails to load or presets are missing, the editor falls back silently: the background may switch to a default imagery source, custom imagery offset is reset, or preset filters are cleared. Check the imagery settings on the task. This is a fallback, not a hard error.

My lock disappeared

> **Needs verification — M-01:** Your lock can be released automatically if you do not submit in time. The system releases stale locks both when the project is next fetched and by a background job. The exact lock duration and background interval are configuration-dependent and have not been verified for this instance.

Support channels

Use the project's Questions and Comments thread to contact the project manager, and check the Learn pages for video tutorials. Guests cannot post comments.

See also

- [Roles and permissions — overview](./05-roles-and-permissions-overview.md)
- [Task states and lifecycle](./03-task-states-and-lifecycle.md)

Sources

- Error code documentation, error messages, exceptions, and permission error modals.

chunks.title: MapSwipe, campaigns, partners, and other project types
chunks.text:
MapSwipe projects

Some projects use task geometries that were imported from an external source such as MapSwipe. These appear as arbitrary task polygons rather than a regular grid. Whether a project has MapSwipe-style tasks is determined when the project is created.

> **Needs verification — M-10:** MapSwipe tasks are created as arbitrary task geometries imported from an external source. Whether a task originated from MapSwipe is determined by how the project was created.

Tasking Manager retrieves MapSwipe statistics via a secured service when configured. MapSwipe project statistics include community contributions and user-group membership. Errors in that service are reported as MapSwipe network or GraphQL errors.

A campaign groups several projects under a theme. Organizations and projects can be associated with campaigns. Campaigns appear as a filter when searching for projects and on project pages where assigned. Only administrators and project managers with the appropriate scope can create or link campaigns. A campaign cannot be assigned twice to the same organization or project.

Partners

Partner pages highlight organizations that collaborate on mapping. Typical partner fields include name, hashtags, logo, permalink, and links. Partner management is an administrative feature; the set of fields that appear to regular mappers versus administrators may vary.

> **Needs verification — M-05:** Partner organizations and their visibility on the project or campaign pages depend on the deployment. Some partner fields are managed only by administrators.

Sandbox and database variants

- **Sandbox** projects are isolated practice projects. They behave like regular projects but are clearly marked as sandbox.
- Most projects use the normal OpenStreetMap database. A small number of projects on specific deployments may target a separate database such as OpenHistoricalMap for historical mapping. The editor still saves edits through the configured OpenStreetMap connection.

See also

- [Creating a new project](../../project-manager/01-creating-a-project.md)
- [System configuration, i18n, and APIs](../../administrator/04-system-configuration.md)
- [Finding work: project discovery and filtering](./08-search-and-discovery.md)

chunks.title: Creating an account, logging in, and managing your profile
chunks.text:
How do I create an account and log in?

You need an OpenStreetMap account. Choose Sign up or Log in in the header, which redirects you to OpenStreetMap to create or authorize your account. After granting the Tasking Manager limited access, you are returned and can start mapping.

> **Needs verification — M-12:** LearnOSM screenshots and older guides may show an earlier Tasking Manager interface. This knowledge base follows the Tasking Manager version described in the current frontend code; some visual differences may exist.

Prerequisites

- A valid OpenStreetMap account and willingness to authorize the Tasking Manager.

Who can log in and who cannot

- **Who can:** Anyone with an OSM account.
- **Who cannot:** Guests who have not logged in cannot lock tasks, comment, or edit. They can still browse public, published projects.

Session and token

Once logged in you receive a session token that authenticates subsequent requests. If the token expires or becomes invalid you will see an authentication error and need to log in again.

Managing your profile

After logging in, open your user menu and choose Settings or view your profile. You can:

- Edit your display name, city, country, picture, gender, social handles, and bio.
- Choose which notifications you receive (mentions, project activity, team broadcasts, task comments, validation of your work).
- Set your preferred editor (iD, JOSM, Potlatch, Field Papers, Rapid, or Custom where available).
- Select interests that help find projects relevant to you.

Who can edit a profile

- **Who can:** You can edit your own profile.
- **Who cannot:** You cannot edit another user's profile; unauthenticated users cannot change profiles.

Email verification

If you add an email address, the system can send you a verification link. Clicking the link confirms your address. Some notification emails depend on verification. Verification links expire.

Expert mode

You can toggle expert mode in your settings. It does not by itself grant extra mapping or validation permissions.

Account deletion and blocking

- You can request deletion of your account, which anonymizes your profile. Upon deletion your personal details are cleared and some associated records are rewritten or removed.

> **Needs verification — M-03:** Account deletion anonymizes your profile to a placeholder name, clears personal details, and removes many associated records. Some related data such as messages and chat entries is rewritten or removed, and some aggregate history may be retained for project statistics. The exact scope follows the deployed version and is not detailed in product documentation.

- Administrators can block a user by setting them to read-only. Blocked users cannot map or validate.

Troubleshooting

- **Invalid token:** Your session expired — log in again.
- **Cannot save profile:** Ensure you are logged in and the field values are valid.

chunks.text:
Reading the project page and selecting a task

> **Needs verification — M-12:** LearnOSM screenshots and older guides may show an earlier Tasking Manager interface. This knowledge base follows the Tasking Manager version described in the current frontend code; some visual differences may exist.

How do I understand the project page?

The project page is organized into sections:

- **Description** — Why the project exists and what area it covers.
- **Instructions** — Exactly what to map, tagging guidance, what imagery to use, and the changeset comment to include.
- **Priority areas** — Highlighted polygons that indicate higher-priority zones within the overall area.
- **Activity** — Recent history of state changes on tasks.
- **Statistics** — Progress bars for mapped and validated percentages, plus totals.

Tip: Read the instructions fully, including the per-task notes if the project provides them, before selecting a task.

How do I select a task?

On the Contribute tab you can either:

- **Pick a task on the map** — Click a task square to select it, or
- **Take a random task** — Let the system choose one for you.

If the project enforces random selection, you must use the random option and cannot choose freely.

Task grid

Tasks are shown as a grid colored by state. A legend explains the colors for Ready, Mapped, Validated, and other states. Priority areas appear as a distinct overlay. You can filter or search tasks within the project by state.

For the meaning of each color and state, see [Task states and lifecycle](../general/03-task-states-and-lifecycle.md).

Prerequisites

- The project must be published and visible to you. Private or draft projects may be hidden. See [Private projects and access control](../general/06-private-projects-and-access-control.md).
- You must meet any level, team, or license requirements the project sets. See [Roles and permissions — overview](../general/05-roles-and-permissions-overview.md).

Permissions — who can select and who cannot

- **Who can:** Mappers who are permitted to map on that project. The checks include project published, license accepted if required, mapper level satisfied, team membership if required, private allowed-list if applicable, and no other lock held.
- **Who cannot:** Guests cannot select for mapping; mappers who already have a task locked cannot select another; mappers below the required level or not in a required team cannot select; mappers not on the allowed list for a private project cannot select.

When blocked, the interface shows a permission reason or you receive an error with a SubCode such as `UserAlreadyHasTaskLocked`, `PrivateProject`, `ProjectNotPublished`, or `UserNotAcceptedLicense`. See [Error codes and troubleshooting](../general/13-error-codes-and-troubleshooting.md).

chunks.title: Mapping a task: lock → edit → save → submit
chunks.text:
Mapping a task: lock → edit → save → submit

> **Needs verification — M-12:** LearnOSM screenshots and older guides may show an earlier Tasking Manager interface. This knowledge base follows the Tasking Manager version described in the current frontend code; some visual differences may exist.

Prerequisites

- You are logged in, the project is published and visible to you, and you satisfy any level, team, or license requirements (see [Roles and permissions — overview](../general/05-roles-and-permissions-overview.md)).
- You have no other task currently locked. You can only hold one lock at a time for mapping or validation.
- The task is in a mappable state (Ready or Invalidated). See [Task states and lifecycle](../general/03-task-states-and-lifecycle.md) for the authoritative list.

Step 1 — Lock a task for mapping

Select a task as described in [Reading the project page and selecting a task](./02-project-page-and-task-selection.md) and choose Lock for mapping.

Who can lock and who cannot

- **Who can:** Mappers who meet the prerequisites above and are permitted to map on that project. See the permission overview for the full decision tree.
- **Who cannot:** Guests; blocked users; users who have not accepted a required license; users below the required mapper level; users not in a required team; users not on the allowed list for a private project; users who already have a task locked. Mappers also cannot lock a task that is already locked by someone else or that is not in Ready/Invalidated. Each case returns a distinct SubCode (`UserAlreadyHasTaskLocked`, `InvalidTaskState`, etc.) — see [Error codes and troubleshooting](../general/13-error-codes-and-troubleshooting.md).

Step 2 — Edit the mapping

The task remains locked while you edit. Save your edits regularly in your editor.

- Use the **changeset comment** suggested on the Instructions tab, keeping the project hashtag (for example `#hotosm-project-1234`). Add a brief note about what you did and the source you used. See [OSM concepts](./../general/02-osm-concepts-for-tasking-manager-users.md).
- Map exactly what the instructions ask for and apply tagging as described in your editor guidance.

For editor choice, imagery, presets, and GPX overlay, see [Editors and imagery](./04-editors-imagery-and-gpx.md).

Step 3 — Submit after mapping

When you have saved to OpenStreetMap, return to the Tasking Manager and submit:

- **Mark as mapped** — Task is complete and ready for validation.
- **Mark as bad imagery** — The imagery prevents mapping (clouds, blur, no coverage). The task will be excluded from progress until a manager resets it.
- **Stop mapping** — Leave the task without marking it complete, optionally leaving a comment. The task returns to its prior state so someone else can work on it.

You can include a comment with your submission; if you mention another user with `@username` they will be notified.

Splitting a task

If a task is very large, you may be offered a split option while it is locked for mapping by you. Splitting divides the task into smaller pieces. Tasks that are already small cannot be split. Splitting is only available while you hold the lock and the geometry is valid.

Restrictions and edge cases

- You cannot merge tasks after they have been split.
- You must hold the lock to submit; submitting a task held by someone else fails with `TaskNotOwned` or `LockBeforeUnlocking`.
- Marking as Bad imagery still requires that you hold the mapping lock, just like marking as Mapped.

chunks.text:
Editors and imagery

> **Needs verification — M-12:** LearnOSM screenshots and older guides may show an earlier Tasking Manager interface. This knowledge base follows the Tasking Manager version described in the current frontend code; some visual differences may exist.

Which editors can I use?

The project specifies which editors are allowed. Common options:

- **iD** — Browser-based, guided, launched from the Tasking Manager.
- **JOSM** — Desktop editor requiring installed JOSM with remote control enabled.
- **Potlatch and Field Papers** — Supported on some projects but less commonly used.
- **Rapid and Custom** — Appear only when the project has been configured to allow them.

You can set a preferred editor in your profile, but the project determines the allowed set.

> **Needs verification — M-11:** The Rapid editor and custom editor options appear only when the project has been configured to allow them. Availability for mappers versus project managers is controlled by the project configuration.

iD editor behavior

When launched, iD loads the task area, locale-appropriate presets, the suggested changeset comment, and any custom imagery or offset configured for the project. The task boundary may appear as an overlay to guide you so you do not edit far outside the task.

For JOSM, ensure remote control is enabled and that your editor can reach the Tasking Manager. Extra editor parameters configured for the project are passed through.

Each project may specify custom imagery — often a TMS URL or template — or fall back to a default such as Bing.

- **Background selection:** Choose the suggested custom imagery or a standard source in the editor.
- **Imagery offset:** Some projects include an offset to align imagery with existing OSM data. The offset is applied when you open the editor and cleared when no offset is configured.
- **Fallbacks:** If imagery is empty, the preset list is missing, or a task download fails, the editor falls back silently: background may switch to the default, offset is reset, preset filters are cleared, or a subtle log is recorded. This is not a hard error — check the imagery menu on the task.

Presets

Projects may limit which presets (feature templates) are available in iD via preset allow-lists. If the preset configuration is missing or malformed, presets reset to the full set.

GPX overlay

Some tasks offer a GPX file of the task boundary to side-load into your editor for guidance. It is loaded as an overlay layer; failure to load shows a message but does not block mapping.

Restrictions

- Using imagery or presets not configured for the project is generally not possible unless the editor allows adding sources manually.
- GPX download errors are non-fatal; you can still map without the overlay.

chunks.title: Comments, task history, and managing your lock
chunks.text:
Comments, task history, and managing your lock

> **Needs verification — M-12:** LearnOSM screenshots and older guides may show an earlier Tasking Manager interface. This knowledge base follows the Tasking Manager version described in the current frontend code; some visual differences may exist.

Task comments and @-mentions

From any task you can leave a comment without changing its state. Guests cannot comment.

If you mention another user with `@username` in a comment, that user receives a mention notification, unless they mentioned themselves or they have disabled that notification category. Use comments to explain what you did, ask for review, or respond to a validator's feedback.

Project-level questions and comments are similar but appear on the project's detail page. Any authenticated user who can view the project can post there; guests cannot.

Task history

Each task shows a history of locks, state changes, comments, extensions, and automatic releases, in chronological order. Use this to understand who worked on the task and what happened, and to find validator feedback on tasks you previously mapped via the project activity or user history.

Extending the lock

If you need more time while a task is locked by you for mapping or validation, you can extend the lock duration where the interface offers it. You must be the lock holder; extending a task locked by someone else fails. The extension is recorded in history.

Auto-release

> **Needs verification — M-01:** Your lock can be released automatically if you do not submit in time. The system releases stale locks both when the project is next fetched and by a background job. The exact lock duration and background interval are configuration-dependent and have not been verified for this instance.

If your lock is auto-released, the task returns to the state it was in before you locked it.

Leaving and resuming

While you have a task locked, it appears in your locked-tasks panel. You can resume mapping from there. You cannot resume a task locked by another user.

Undoing the last action

If you or a validator made the most recent state change on a task, you may be able to undo it. What happens:

- Validated → returns to Mapped
- Bad imagery → returns to Ready
- Mapped → returns to Ready
- Otherwise, the previous state is restored from history

Undo is blocked if you were not the last actor and you are not a validator for that task.

Permissions — who can do what

- **Who can comment:** Any authenticated user who can view the task/project.
- **Who cannot comment:** Guests.
- **Who can extend a lock:** The holder of a Locked for mapping or Locked for validation lock. Not the case for tasks you do not hold.
- **Who can undo:** The author of the last state change or a validator on that task.

chunks.title: Creating a new project
chunks.text:
Creating a new project

> **Needs verification — M-12:** LearnOSM screenshots and older guides may show an earlier Tasking Manager interface. This knowledge base follows the Tasking Manager version described in the current frontend code; some visual differences may exist.

Who can create

- **Who can:** Organization managers for the chosen organization and Tasking Manager administrators.
- **Who cannot:** Regular mappers, validators, or team members who are not organization managers cannot create projects.

Attempts by non-managers return a NotPermittedToCreate error.

Step 1 — Define the area of interest (AOI)

You can define the AOI in two ways:

- **Draw on the map** — Use the drawing tools to trace a polygon tightly around the area you want mapped. Tightly framing the AOI reduces empty edge tasks.
- **Upload a file** — Import a GeoJSON, KML, or zipped shapefile containing the AOI or task geometries. You can also import pre-defined task polygons (for example a grid prepared in GIS or tasks from a MapSwipe import) by enabling the option to use uploaded polygons as tasks.

> **Needs verification — M-07:** File size limits for uploading an area of interest or task grid are not documented in the sources. Very large files may be rejected — try simplifying the geometry and splitting the area into smaller projects.

**Recommendations:** Keep a project under about 1,000 km² so it completes efficiently. The technical limit is around 5,000 km²; larger areas should be split into multiple projects.

Step 2 — Define tasks

By default the area is divided into a regular grid. You can:

- **Resize tasks** — Use Larger and Smaller to adjust the overall size. Aim for a size that a confident mapper can finish in about 15 minutes, accounting for feature density (dense urban areas need smaller tasks than rural roads).
- **Selectively split** — Click to split specific tasks into four smaller pieces, or draw an area to split all tasks within it. The reset option clears custom splits.
- **Trim to the AOI** — Remove tasks that do not overlap the AOI, optionally clipping overlapping edge tasks exactly to the AOI outline. Very tiny clipped tasks below about 2,000 m² can be discarded.

Tasks can be split but not merged after creation.

Step 3 — Assign organization and campaign

Choose the organization that will own the project and optionally link one or more campaigns that group related projects.

- **Who can assign:** The creator who is an organization manager for that organization.

Step 4 — Changeset comment

Each project has a default changeset comment that includes a hashtag like `#hotosm-project-1234` plus any custom text you add. The system prefixes your custom text with the project's default hashtag when you save.

chunks.text:
Configuring a project

> **Needs verification — M-12:** LearnOSM screenshots and older guides may show an earlier Tasking Manager interface. This knowledge base follows the Tasking Manager version described in the current frontend code; some visual differences may exist.

Overview

Configuration is done from the Project Edit view. Only the project author, organization managers for the owning organization, assigned team managers with the Project Manager role for that project, and administrators can edit.

- **Who can:** Managers for that project.
- **Who cannot:** Regular mappers or validators cannot edit. Attempts return a permission error.

General information (per language)

Projects store information separately for each language:

- **Name, short description, description, instructions, and optional per-task instructions** — Required fields in the project's default language must all be provided before publishing, especially name, short description, description, and instructions.
- **Per-task instructions** — Optional additional guidance shown within a specific task.

If the default language information is incomplete, publishing fails.

Status, priority, difficulty, and dates

- **Status:** Draft, Published, or Archived. See [Project status and lifecycle](../../general/04-project-lifecycle-and-status.md).
- **Priority:** Urgent, High, Medium, or Low.
- **Difficulty:** Easy, Moderate, or Challenging — helps mappers choose appropriate projects.
- **Due date:** Optional target date.

License, campaign, and country

- **License:** If a data license is selected, mappers must accept it before mapping. The license must exist; an unknown license identifier blocks save.
- **Campaign and country tags:** Optional groupings that help discovery.

Mapping types and interests

Select which feature categories the project expects (roads, buildings, waterways, land use, other) and any interest topics. At least one mapping type must be selected.

For tagging expectations per type, see [Tagging, presets, and quality assurance](../../validator/03-quality-assurance-and-tagging.md).

Priority areas

Draw polygons to highlight higher-priority sub-areas inside the overall AOI. These appear as a distinct overlay on the mapper's task grid.

Imagery, presets, and editors

- **Imagery:** A custom imagery URL or template, or the default. Imagery is consumed by mappers in their editor. A TMS URL starting with http is used as a template; otherwise a named imagery source is selected.
- **Imagery offset:** Optional `extra_id_params` can include an offset to align imagery with existing data.
- **iD presets and JOSM preset:** Allow-lists of feature templates. Malformed lists are ignored and fall back to the full set.
- **Editors:** Choose which editors are allowed for mapping and for validation (iD, JOSM, Potlatch, Field Papers, Custom, Rapid). At least one must be allowed for each, and a custom editor URL is required if Custom is selected.
- **Rapid and custom editor:** Manage name, URL, and description for a custom editor such as Rapid.

> **Needs verification — M-11:** The Rapid editor and custom editor options appear only when the project has been configured to allow them. Availability for mappers versus project managers is controlled by the project configuration.

Additional settings

- **OSMCha filter ID** — Optional filter for validator QA linking.
- **Enforce random task selection** — When enabled, mappers must pick tasks at random and cannot freely choose.
- **Default language** — The language used when a requested locale is not available.
- **Mapping and validation editors:** configured separately.

Publishing checklist

Before publishing, ensure: default-language fields are filled, at least one mapping type is selected, editors allow at least one choice, organization is set, and any required license is valid. Missing fields produce a validation message naming the missing item.

chunks.title: Project permissions and teams (authoritative applied view)
chunks.text:
Project permissions and teams (authoritative applied view)

This is the authoritative applied view for *how to configure* project permissions. The decision trees live in [Roles and permissions — overview](../../general/05-roles-and-permissions-overview.md); this page shows the knobs.

The permission block

Projects expose a permission block with:

- **Mapping permission:** Anyone (ANY) or Only team members (TEAMS).
- **Validation permission:** Anyone or Only team members (with validator-specific team checks).
- **Minimum mapping/validation levels:** Beginner, Intermediate, Advanced.
- **Private flag** and **allowed users** list.
- **Team assignments** per role.

Mapping and validation team restrictions

- When mapping permission is set to Teams, at least one team assigned to the project as Mappers (or also Validators/Project Managers) must exist; otherwise the project cannot be saved.
- When validation permission is set to Teams, at least one team assigned as Validators or Project Managers must exist. A team assigned only as Mappers does not satisfy validation.

The interface prevents saving with the reason `noTeamsAssigned` if the required team is missing.

Levels

Each project sets a minimum mapping level and a separate minimum validation level. Mappers and validators must meet or exceed the relevant threshold. Level ordering is defined by the mapper level configuration.

See [Mapper levels and badges](../../general/07-mapper-levels-and-badges.md).

Private and allowed users

When a project is private, you can list specific users who are explicitly allowed. That list is combined with assigned teams, the author, organization managers, and administrators to determine who can view the project. Being on the allowed list is not sufficient for mapping or validating if level or team requirements are not met.

See [Private projects and access control](../../general/06-private-projects-and-access-control.md).

Team assignments

- You can link a team to the project as Mapper, Validator, Project Manager, or Read-only.
- A team can be linked multiple times with different roles, but the same team cannot be linked twice with the same role in the same project — the interface reports `duplicateTeamsAssigned` and blocks save.
- Removing a team-project link is allowed only when that link exists; otherwise a not-found error is returned.

Editor whitelist and related toggles

Chosen editors for mapping and validation, custom editor details, and the `Enforce random task selection` toggle are part of the same configuration screen. At least one editor must be allowed for each of mapping and validation; selecting Custom without a URL blocks save.

Who can configure

- **Who can:** Project author, organization managers for the owning organization, assigned team managers with the Project Manager role for that project, and administrators.
- **Who cannot:** Regular mappers, validators who are not managers for that project, and team members with only Mapper or Validator roles cannot edit configuration.
