Managing a project through its lifecycle

> **Needs verification — M-12:** LearnOSM screenshots and older guides may show an earlier Tasking Manager interface. This knowledge base follows the Tasking Manager version described in the current frontend code; some visual differences may exist.

Save, test, and publish

After configuring, save and test. Publishing runs validation that checks the default language information, mapping types, editors, organization, and license. Missing items produce an explanatory error. Draft projects are only visible to managers, as described in [Project status and lifecycle](../../general/04-project-lifecycle-and-status.md).

Cloning a project

Cloning creates a draft copy with its area, tasks, and settings reused. You become the author of the clone; it must be published separately. You can optionally mark the clone as sandbox or target a different database.

- **Who can clone:** Organization managers and administrators who can create projects.
- **Who cannot:** Mappers and validators who are not organization managers.

Featuring and unfeaturing

Project managers can feature a project to highlight it on discovery pages, and unfeature it to remove the highlight. Idempotency checks prevent featuring an already featured project or unfeaturing one that is not featured.

Transferring ownership

Project ownership can be transferred to another user who is an organization manager for the owning organization or an administrator. The transfer is transactional and a notification is sent to the new owner.

- **Who can transfer:** Administrators, the current author, or organization managers for the owning organization.
- **Who cannot:** Other mappers or team members. If the current user is not permitted, the error is a permission error; if the new owner is not a manager or administrator, the error indicates invalid new owner.

Bulk operations

Project managers and administrators can run bulk actions that affect many tasks while preserving history and adjusting counters:

- **Map all tasks** — marks eligible tasks as mapped.
- **Validate all mapped tasks** — marks mapped tasks as validated.
- **Invalidate all validated tasks** — marks validated tasks as invalidated.
- **Reset all bad imagery** — returns tasks marked Bad imagery to Ready and resets the bad-imagery counter.
- **Reset all tasks** — returns tasks to Ready while preserving history and zeroing progress counters.

Regular mappers cannot run these actions.

Messaging

Project managers can send a broadcast message to all contributors who have mapped or validated on that project. The message is formatted from Markdown and sent in the background. Only managers for that project can broadcast.

Project questions and comments from mappers appear on the project's detail page; managers can respond there.

Deletion

A project can only be deleted when it has no completed work — that is, every task is still Ready. If any task is in another state, deletion is blocked. Only organization managers and administrators can delete.

chunks.title: Validating tasks
chunks.text:
Validating tasks

> **Needs verification — M-12:** LearnOSM screenshots and older guides may show an earlier Tasking Manager interface. This knowledge base follows the Tasking Manager version described in the current frontend code; some visual differences may exist.

Prerequisites

- You are logged in and permitted to validate on that project. Validation often requires a higher mapper level than mapping (commonly Intermediate), license acceptance if the project requires it, and team membership if validation is team-restricted. See [Roles and permissions — overview](../general/05-roles-and-permissions-overview.md).
- The task is in a state that can be validated: Mapped, Bad imagery, or Invalidated.
- You have no other task currently locked. Mapping and validation share a single lock budget — holding a task for mapping blocks locking another for validation and vice-versa.

For the meaning of each state, see [Task states and lifecycle](../general/03-task-states-and-lifecycle.md).

1. Lock tasks for validation

Select one or more tasks that are Mapped, Bad imagery, or Invalidated and choose Lock for validation.

2. Review and then unlock

- **Mark as validated** — The mapping is satisfactory.
- **Mark as invalidated** — The mapping has issues that need fixing. Include a comment explaining what to correct and, where the interface offers it, choose mapping-issue categories with counts.
- **Stop validating** — Release the lock without marking, returning the task to its prior state (for example Mapped).

You can add a comment when unlocking. If you validated or invalidated, the original mapper is notified unless you are notifying yourself.

Who can validate and who cannot

- **Who can:** Validators who satisfy the project's level, license, team (Validators or Project Managers), and private/draft visibility checks, and who are not already holding another lock, and who did not do the original mapping. Only administrators may validate their own mapped tasks — project managers, organization managers, and other validators cannot.
- **Who cannot:** Guests; blocked users; users below the required level; users not in a required validator team; users not on the allowed list for a private project; users who already have a task locked; users trying to validate a task they mapped. Only administrators may validate their own mapped task — project managers and other validators receive `CannotValidateMappedTask` (403) when attempting to self-validate. Validators also cannot lock tasks that are not Mapped, Bad imagery, or Invalidated.

Failures return distinct SubCodes such as `CannotValidateMappedTask` (self-validation), `NotReadyForValidation`, or `UserAlreadyHasTaskLocked`. See [Error codes and troubleshooting](../general/13-error-codes-and-troubleshooting.md).

Self-validation guard

The Tasking Manager prevents you from validating a task you mapped yourself. The reason shown is that tasks cannot be validated by the same user who marked the task as mapped or bad imagery. The check compares the mapped-by user to the validator; only administrators bypass it — this is separate from the broader project-manager permission that lets managers validate *other* users' tasks. Project managers, organization managers, and other validators cannot self-validate and will receive `CannotValidateMappedTask`.

After validation

The mapper is notified of the result. Invalidated tasks return to the mapping queue and can be remapped. Validated tasks contribute to validated progress on the project.

chunks.title: Mapping issues and invalidation history
chunks.text:
Mapping issue categories

When a validator marks a task as invalidated, they can record **mapping issues** with counts per category — for example, buildings not traced or roads misaligned — to explain what needs correction. The categories are managed by the system; project managers select which categories are available.

- **Who can annotate issues:** Validators who are unlocking a task as Invalidated.
- **When:** Only during the Invalidated transition is the issue payload recorded. Validated transitions do not carry mapping issues.

Invalidation history lifecycle

Each invalidation creates an **invalidation history entry** that tracks:

- Who mapped the task and when,
- Who invalidated it and when,
- Whether the issue has been closed,
- Who later re-validated it.

An open entry is created when a task is invalidated. It remains open (`is_closed = false`) until a validator later marks that task as validated, which closes the entry. Duplicate open entries are handled by keeping only the most recent — older duplicates are closed automatically.

Invalidation history powers follow-ups such as per-user invalidated-task lists.

Bulk operations for managers

Project managers and administrators can perform bulk actions that affect validation state across many tasks while preserving history:

- **Invalidate all validated tasks** — resets validated counters.
- **Validate all mapped tasks** — promotes mapped tasks to validated.
- **Reset all bad imagery** — returns tasks marked bad imagery to Ready and resets the bad-imagery counter.
- **Reset all tasks** — preserves history but returns tasks to Ready and zeroes progress counters.

These are manager-only actions. Regular mappers cannot run them.

chunks.text:
Tagging expectations

Each project's instructions describe what to map and how to tag it — for example, buildings as closed polygons, roads as lines, waterways, or land use. The tagging scheme follows the OSM Wiki Map Features. Using the expected tags makes data consistent for humanitarian and community use.

- **Project managers** choose which mapping types a project uses.
- **Mappers and validators** follow the per-task instructions and recommended presets.

Presets

Projects may curate preset allow-lists for editors:

- **iD presets** — The set of feature templates offered in iD during mapping.
- **JOSM preset** — A preset file for JOSM.

Projects may also include a data license that you must accept before mapping or validating. If the preset configuration is malformed or absent, the editor falls back to the full set.

OSMCha and quality assurance

**OSMCha** is an external tool for inspecting changesets, often filtered by the project's changeset hashtag. Project managers may configure an **OSMCha filter ID** for a project; a button on the project page then links validators directly to the relevant OSMCha view for that project.

Validators should also be aware of general QA expectations described in OSM Wiki Quality Assurance — for example, checking for overlapping buildings, duplicated roads, and appropriate tagging.

See also

- [OSM concepts for Tasking Manager users](../../general/02-osm-concepts-for-tasking-manager-users.md)
